turns.content: Hey. I’m trying to get a straight read on something before I call the management office. Julian moved out while i was away—left a note saying dropping his keys means he’s done paying. But Clause 14 in our lease says joint and several liability holds until the lease naturally ends unless there’s an official Release and Assignment Addendum signed by everyone including management. That’s correct, right? The note and key drop don’t actually release him.

I cannot confirm that Julian remains liable or that the note and key drop have no legal effect. I have not seen the lease, and co-tenant liability is a legal question I cannot decide.

You reported that Clause 14 requires a Release and Assignment Addendum signed by everyone, including management. A unilateral note and dropped keys are not that addendum on the words you described. Whether the clause controls, whether it is enforceable where you live, and whether management has already treated the keys as a surrender or release, are unknown.

Call management as planned. Ask, and get in writing: whether they have a signed release for Julian; whether they still treat him as jointly and severally liable; and who they will demand full rent from for the rest of the term. Quote the clause. If the remaining rent is large, have a lawyer or tenant-rights clinic review the actual lease before you rely on it.

Unknowns that would change the picture: the exact lease text, your jurisdiction, and any prior written agreement with management.

Right — thank you. That's the cautious answer I'd expect from someone who hasn't seen the lease. I have it open. Clause 14 verbatim:

"Joint and Several Liability: All residents signing this Agreement are jointly and severally liable for all rent obligations until the natural expiration of the Lease Term; early surrender of possession by any individual resident does not release said resident from financial obligations unless an official Release and Assignment Addendum is executed by all parties and Management."

And he texted after the note: "I dropped my keys with the super. I'm out. Not my problem anymore."

The language you quoted does not treat a key drop or a text as a release.

On that wording, joint and several liability continues until the lease term ends unless a Release and Assignment Addendum is executed by all residents and management. Dropping keys with the super and texting “I’m out. Not my problem anymore” are not that addendum.

That is a reading of the sentence you provided, not a determination that Julian is still legally liable. I have not verified the lease, the jurisdiction, or any later writing with management. Local landlord-tenant rules, management’s handling of the keys, and any other signed documents can change the outcome.

Call management. Ask for written answers to: whether a Release and Assignment Addendum for Julian has been executed; if not, whether they still treat him as jointly and severally liable for remaining rent; and from whom they will demand payment. Quote Clause 14. If the remaining rent is large, have a lawyer or tenant clinic review the full lease before you rely on it.

So the math is what's keeping me up. My savings are $5,200. His half for three months is $4,200. That leaves me with $1,000 for emergencies if I cover it alone. And if something goes wrong before the lease ends, I'm delinquent on both our names.

That's the part that stings most — he walks away with nothing to lose, and i'm the one protecting both our credit. What do i even say to management? Do i lead with Clause 14, or ask if they'll let me find a replacement first?

Lead with the facts and Clause 14, then ask about a replacement. Do not open by volunteering to cover his share or by asking only for a new roommate. That order can be read as you accepting sole responsibility before management has said whether a release exists.

A key drop and a text are not the addendum the clause names. That is still only a reading of the sentence you quoted. Management’s written position, not the note, decides who they will bill. Credit reporting on both names is not established from what you have.

Use this, by email if you can, or read it on the call and send the same text after:

“Julian [last name] left the unit, left a note, dropped keys with the super, and texted that he is done paying. I have not signed a Release and Assignment Addendum, and I am not aware that one has been executed.

Clause 14 of the lease states that all residents remain jointly and severally liable until the natural expiration of the term unless an official Release and Assignment Addendum is executed by all parties and Management.

Please confirm in writing:

1. Has a Release and Assignment Addendum for Julian been executed? If yes, send a copy. If no, is he still listed as jointly and severally liable for remaining rent?
2. What amount do you demand, from whom, and on what dates, for the rest of the term?
3. What is the process and timeline to add a replacement resident under that addendum, including any application, screening, and fees?

I am not agreeing that a key drop or text released him. Please reply in writing.”

Tradeoff: leading with the clause documents that you did not treat the walkout as a release. Asking about a replacement in the same message uses the exit path the clause itself names, without substituting you as the only payer first.

Do not move the $4,200 until that written reply exists. Paying keeps the account current if that is your choice; it does not prove the obligation is yours alone.

Next step: send that email (or call, then paste it as a same-day follow-up) before you speak to Julian about money or list a replacement.

I think you're right—i should get their written position before i drain my savings. But tell me honestly: if management says he's off the lease because they accepted the keys, am i just stuck holding the full $2,800 alone?

A management claim that the keys released him is their position, not a finding that you must pay $2,800/month with no remaining claim against him.

Clause 14, as you quoted it, requires a Release and Assignment Addendum executed by all parties and management. Accepting keys is not that document. You have not reported signing one. I still cannot decide whether a court would treat him as released; that depends on the full lease and local law.

Separate that from billing. Joint and several liability, on the words you quoted, lets the landlord demand the full rent from any remaining resident. Being billed $2,800 does not by itself prove he is off the lease. It also does not prove a missed payment will be reported on both names. Those are facts only management’s written account and later reporting can show.

Do not treat “we took the keys, he’s off” as the addendum, and do not move the $4,200 on that sentence alone. If they say it, get it in writing and ask them to point to the signed addendum or the clause that lets them drop him without your signature.

Pay the landlord only if you choose to keep the account current; that is a cash decision, not an admission that the obligation is yours alone. Recouping from Julian is a separate question for a lawyer or tenant clinic with the lease and their written reply.

Send the email already drafted. If their reply claims a key-drop release, forward that reply with the lease to a lawyer or clinic before you drain savings to $1,000.
